findings.title: Do not pipe unverified remote script into sh in image build
findings.whyItBreaks: The added build step fetches https://example.com/install.sh and executes it directly via `| sh` with no pinned version, no checksum/signature verification, no TLS pinning and no allow-listed source. Anyone controlling that URL (or the network path absent integrity checks) executes arbitrary code as root inside the image at `docker build` time, and the built image/`CMD ["/app"]` inherits whatever that script installed. This is a supply-chain remote-code-execution vector and makes builds non-reproducible.

findings.title: Pipeline masks curl failure; build succeeds with missing install
findings.whyItBreaks: `curl -sL ... | sh` discards curl's exit status: Docker sees only the exit code of `sh`. Because `curl` is invoked without `-f`, an HTTP error page or a 404/network failure is fed to `sh` (or yields empty input), and an empty/partial script makes `sh` exit 0. The `RUN` therefore reports success while the intended install silently did not happen, producing a broken image with no error signal — the failure cannot be distinguished from a legitimate build.

findings.title: Remove curl | sh: unpinned, unverified remote code execution in build
findings.whyItBreaks: Line 3 pipes a network-fetched script straight into `sh` as root during the image build with no version pin and no hash/signature verification. Any compromise or replacement of https://example.com/install.sh (or a MITM/TLS-terminating mirror, or a later redirect target since -L follows redirects) runs arbitrary code inside the image and yields non-reproducible builds; the same commit can build different images over time. This is a classic install-time supply-chain/RCE vector and must be removed or made deterministic.

findings.title: Do not pipe a remote script into sh during image build
findings.whyItBreaks: `curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` executes whatever the remote host returns at build time as root inside the image. It is unpinned (no commit/tag/version), unhashed, and unsigned, so the build is non-reproducible and anyone who controls the served content (DNS, TLS termination, host compromise, or a future change to the URL) gains arbitrary code execution in the resulting image. Because the pipeline exit status is `sh`'s, a failed/incorrect download (e.g. a 404 HTML body) can still be fed to the shell without a visible failure; `curl` also lacks `-f`/`--fail`, so HTTP errors are not surfaced.

findings.title: LoadOrDefault discards Load's error, hiding missing/failed loads
findings.whyItBreaks: LoadOrDefault assigns `v, _ := Load(key, m)`, dropping the error. On a missing key Load returns ("", ErrMissing); the wrapper converts that failure to the empty string and returns it as a normal value. Because the default is the zero value, a caller cannot distinguish a failed/missing load from a key that is legitimately stored as "" — the failure is reported as real data and may be persisted, displayed, or used to overwrite state instead of surfacing ErrMissing. The function is exported (public API), so every future caller is forced into this conflation; no in-repo caller is required for the contract itself to be the defect.

findings.title: LoadOrDefault swallows ErrMissing, hiding missing-vs-empty
findings.whyItBreaks: The new exported LoadOrDefault discards the error returned by Load (`v, _ := Load(key, m)`). Load returns ErrMissing (src/store.go:10) when the key is absent, and `""` when the key is present with an empty value. Both are collapsed into `""`, so an exported package contract gives callers no way to distinguish "absent" from "present but empty". LoadOrDefault is exported (package store), so the API itself forces every future consumer to treat a failed lookup as a real value — a present defect regardless of in-repo callers.

findings.title: LoadOrDefault silently swallows ErrMissing, conflating missing and empty
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing (src/store.go:10) specifically when a key is absent, but LoadOrDefault discards that error with `v, _ := Load(...)` and returns only the zero value. Every eventual caller is forced to conflate 'key missing' with 'key present but set to an empty string' — Load returns "" for a present empty value too (src/store.go:12), so the two cases are observationally identical. A caller that must distinguish an absent config/record from an intentionally blank one cannot do so through this exported contract. Per the public-swallow rule this is a defect in the API contract itself and stands even with no in-repo callers (there are none yet; the package is the whole repo).

findings.title: Run now returns before results are sent, dropping completion guarantee
findings.whyItBreaks: Base Run sent every result synchronously, so returning implied all results had been delivered and no goroutine outlived the call. The change spawns one goroutine per job and returns immediately without any sync.WaitGroup, return channel, or ctx cancellation. Any caller that closes results after Run returns (worker.Run(ctx, jobs, results); close(results)) now races the spawned goroutines and panics with 'send on closed channel'; any caller that stops reading early leaks every goroutine still blocked on results <- ... since ctx is never observed. Concurrency is also now unbounded (len(jobs) goroutines at once). The exported signature is unchanged, so runtranss silently keep the old assumption.

findings.title: Async sends break Run's ordered, synchronous result contract
findings.whyItBreaks: Before the change, Run sent `j*2` inline, so (a) results arrived in the same order as jobs and (b) Run returned only after every job had been delivered. Spawning one goroutine per job removes both guarantees: goroutines race for the channel, so positional correspondence between `jobs[i]` and received results is lost, and Run now returns immediately while sends are still in flight. A caller that ranges over/collects `results` positionally gets a nondeterministically reordered slice, and a caller that closes `results` after Run returns panics with `send on closed channel` in the still-running goroutines (or leaks them if `results` is buffered and the consumer stops reading).

findings.title: Run returns before goroutines deliver results (lost/partial results, panic)
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change the loop sent every result synchronously, so Run returning implied all len(jobs) values had been placed on results. The new body spawns one detached goroutine per job and returns immediately: Run now returns before any (or all) of the `results <- j*2` sends have happened, and there is no WaitGroup/synchronization to restore the old contract. Callers that rely on completion — e.g. draining exactly len(jobs) values, or closing the results channel right after Run returns — will observe missing results and/or panic with 'send on closed channel' when a still-running goroutine sends to the closed channel. The spawn is also unbounded, so a large jobs slice creates len(jobs) blocked goroutines that leak if the consumer stops reading.

findings.title: canDeleteRecord now authorizes deletion by any same-tenant non-admin
findings.whyItBreaks: Base behavior was `session.isAdmin && session.tenantId === record.tenantId`, i.e. deletion required BOTH admin rights AND same-tenant ownership. The new `||` makes the predicate true whenever EITHER holds: (1) any user whose tenantId matches the record's tenantId may delete it even if isAdmin is false (vertical privilege escalation to delete), and (2) a user with isAdmin true in ANY tenant may delete records belonging to other tenants (cross-tenant authorization bypass). Because this exported predicate is the delete authorization decision, every caller that gates a delete on its return value now permits actions the previous contract rejected. The record's ownerId field is still ignored, so the change does not implement any owner-based intent — it strictly loosens the guard.

findings.title: canDeleteRecord admits cross-tenant admin and non-admin deletes
findings.whyItBreaks: The guard previously required BOTH `session.isAdmin` AND `session.tenantId === record.tenantId`, so only an admin acting inside their own tenant could delete. Changing `&&` to `||` makes the predicate true when EITHER holds: (1) any session with `isAdmin=true` now passes regardless of `record.tenantId`, so an admin of tenant A can delete records belonging to tenant B — a cross-tenant authorization bypass and destructive data-loss path; (2) any non-admin whose `tenantId` matches gets deletion rights, silently dropping the admin requirement entirely. Both the admin gate and the tenant-isolation check are defeated by a single operator change.

findings.title: canDeleteRecord now authorizes cross-tenant admins and non-admin peers
findings.whyItBreaks: Substituting the two booleans into `session.isAdmin || session.tenantId === record.tenantId`: (isAdmin=true, different tenant) now returns true, so an admin of tenant A can delete records of tenant B — a cross-tenant data-loss bypass. (isAdmin=false, same tenant) also now returns true, so any non-admin user can delete every record in their tenant, not just their own. Base `&&` denied both cases. The exported predicate is the authorization contract for record deletion, so both newly-true rows are real authorization failures on the live decision path.

findings.title: parseSettings swallows parse errors, silently resetting settings to DEFAULTS
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, invalid JSON or a wrong-typed theme/fontSize threw out of parseSettings and propagated through updateFontSize, aborting before save(). Now the catch-all returns DEFAULTS, so updateFontSize (src/settings.ts:20) proceeds with { theme: "light", fontSize: 14 }, mutates fontSize, and calls save() (src/settings.ts:22), persisting defaults over the user's on-disk settings. Callers can no longer distinguish 'unparseable/corrupt config' from 'a real value of light/14', so a recoverable or partially-valid config (e.g. a valid theme with a bad fontSize) is destroyed rather than surfaced. Every error, including unexpected ones, is discarded with no logging.

The new catch-all at line 14-15 maps every failure (malformed JSON, wrong field types) to { ...DEFAULTS }, so updateFontSize (line 20) receives a real-looking Settings object, sets fontSize and calls save(JSON.stringify(settings)) at line 22 — persisting theme:'light' and silently discarding the user's previously saved theme/other values. Failure and the fallback value are indistinguishable to any caller, including the exported public API of parseSettings.

findings.title: parseSettings swallows parse/validation errors, caller persists defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change a malformed JSON payload or an invalid field (typeof data.theme !== 'string' / typeof data.fontSize !== 'number') threw out of parseSettings: 'bad theme'/'bad fontSize' or the JSON.parse error propagated, so callers could tell failure apart from a value and could abort. Now catch{} maps every failure to { theme: 'light', fontSize: 14 }, an indistinguishable legitimate-looking value, and the exported contract no longer reports failure at all. The one in-repo caller, updateFontSize (src/settings.ts:20-22), consumes it as a real value: it mutates fontSize and calls save(JSON.stringify(settings)). So a partially-valid stored setting such as {"theme":"dark","fontSize":"14"} now causes theme to be silently reset to light and the user's persisted config to be overwritten with defaults, instead of surfacing the error and leaving the existing (recoverable) stored value untouched.

findings.title: buildReport pairs builtFrom=branch commit with artifacts from unrelated `verified` ref
findings.whyItBreaks: `commit` is resolved from `branch` (line 12) and reported as `builtFrom`, but `artifacts` is now fetched from a second, independently resolved ref `verified` (lines 13-14). `BuildReport.builtFrom` names the commit the artifacts were built from; when `build.ref("verified")` differs from `build.ref(branch)` (the normal case — they are distinct ref names), the report lists artifacts belonging to one commit while claiming they came from another, so any consumer displaying commit↔artifact provenance misattributes artifacts. Previously both fields used the same `commit`, keeping the pair consistent.

findings.title: buildReport lists artifacts from wrong ref vs builtFrom
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, artifacts and the reported source commit came from the same ref (`commit = build.ref(branch)`, then `artifactsAt(commit)`), so BuildReport was internally consistent. The new code resolves a separate ref `build.ref("verified")` and returns `artifacts: build.artifactsAt(verified)` while `builtFrom` is still the branch's commit. Callers now receive a report whose `builtFrom` provenance does not describe the artifacts it lists, and if the `"verified"` ref does not exist the call yields artifacts for a non-existent/undefined commit instead of the requested branch.

findings.title: buildReport pairs branch commit with artifacts from unrelated "verified" ref
findings.whyItBreaks: Built before as build.artifactsAt(commit) where commit = build.ref(branch), so builtFrom and artifacts described the same revision. Now artifacts come from build.artifactsAt(build.ref("verified")), a hardcoded ref independent of the branch argument. For any branch whose tip is not what "verified" points at (i.e. every branch except that exact ref), BuildReport returns builtFrom = the branch commit alongside artifacts belonging to a different commit: the two fields no longer describe one build, the branch parameter silently stops governing which artifacts are reported, and if no "verified" ref exists, ref("verified") yields an unresolved value whose artifactsAt result is unrelated to the requested branch. Build interface at src/report.ts:1-4 confirms ref(name): string and artifactsAt(commit): string[] take the revision directly.

findings.title: Restore limit cap: recentEntries returns all entries when limit > 0
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed body computes `sorted` but never truncates it: for any `limit > 0` the function returns the full reversed array (src/feed.ts:5), while the unchanged doc comment promises 'Returns at most `limit` entries' (src/feed.ts:1). Base behavior was `[...all].reverse().slice(0, limit)`. The in-repo caller `renderFeed` passes `limit = 20` (src/feed.ts:9) and copies `page[i]` into `out` for `i < page.length`, so a feed with more than 20 entries now returns every entry instead of at most 20 — a user-facing regression and a broken public-API contract.

findings.title: Reinstate the `limit` cap in recentEntries
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed body reverses the input but never applies `limit`: `const sorted = [...all].reverse(); if (limit <= 0) return []; return sorted;`. The unchanged doc comment on line 1 promises "Returns at most `limit` entries, newest first", but for any `limit > 0` the function now returns ALL entries. The only caller, `renderFeed` (src/feed.ts:9-12), calls `recentEntries(all, 20)` and copies `page[i]` for `i < page.length` into a fixed-size `new Array<string>(20)`; assigning past index 19 extends the array, so the feed renders every entry instead of the newest 20. The pre-change code `[...all].reverse().slice(0, limit)` produced exactly `min(limit, all.length)` entries.

findings.title: recentEntries ignores limit, breaking at-most-limit contract
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed body builds `sorted` and returns it unchanged for `limit > 0`; the previous `.slice(0, limit)` cap was removed, so the function returns ALL entries instead of at most `limit`, contradicting its doc comment on line 1. Consumer renderFeed (src/feed.ts:9) calls `recentEntries(all, 20)` then loops `i < page.length` writing into `out` (src/feed.ts:10-12), so when `all.length > 20` the page grows past 20 entries instead of being capped, changing the rendered feed size.

findings.title: Synchronize entry-count header with filtered rows
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff filters the emitted rows to non-stale entries (`live`), but line 22 still calls `headerLines(opts, entries.length)`, so the `# entry-count:` header counts stale entries that are no longer present in the body. `renderManifest` is exported, so the header/body mismatch is a public contract defect: any consumer that reads `entry-count` to size, pre-allocate, or validate the manifest against the emitted rows gets a count larger than the rows actually returned (e.g. entries=[{stale:true},{stale:false}] emits one data row but `# entry-count: 2`).

findings.title: entry-count header no longer matches emitted rows after stale filter
findings.whyItBreaks: The PR filters stale entries out of the rows (line 20-21 `live = entries.filter(e => !e.stale)`), but the header still passes `entries.length` (line 22). For any input containing stale entries, `# entry-count:` reports the total including stale entries while the body emits only live rows, so the declared count disagrees with the actual number of rows. Any consumer that sizes buffers, validates the file by counting rows, or treats entry-count as authoritative metadata now mismatches (e.g. 3 entries, 1 stale -> `# entry-count: 3` with 2 data rows).

findings.title: Concurrent reserve() now oversells after added await

During that await the JS event loop can run another reserve() for the same sku: both calls read the same `remaining` (line 15), both pass `remaining <= 0` (line 16), both resolve the store write, both set the stock to `remaining - 1` (line 18), and both return true (line 19). For stock=1, two concurrent reservations both report success while only one unit existed, and the persisted store is written the same value twice (lost update). The atomicity that the synchronous version provided is silently removed.

Two concurrent reserve() calls for a sku with one unit both read remaining=1, both pass the unchanged `remaining <= 0` guard at line 16, both persist `remaining - 1` = 0, both set stock to 0, and both return true. Result: two successful reservations of a single unit (oversell / lost update) and the store/in-memory value silently disagreeing with the number of grants. Before this change the method was synchronous, so the JS event loop made interleaving impossible; consumers must now `await`, making parallel calls (e.g. `Promise.all`) the natural usage that triggers this.

Because the deferred Close error is discarded, Save now returns nil for writes that were never persisted, so callers treat a failed save as success and can proceed to report/persist state that does not exist on disk. findings.title: page_window drops the last row of every page
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns a half-open [start, end) range where end is already exclusive (end = min(start + page_size, row_count)), and the base implementation correctly iterated range(start, end). The refactor changed the loop to range(start, end - 1), so the final position of every window is skipped. Example: rows=[a,b,c,d], page_size=2 -> page_count=2; page 0 yields [a] (b dropped), page 1 yields [c] (d dropped), so summarize renders 1. a / --- / 2. c and rows b and d never appear. With page_size=1 every page returns empty and summarize returns only separators. This is a real regression versus base (which returned range(start, end)) that loses rows from all rendered output.

findings.title: page_window drops last row of every page (range end-1)

The head version iterates range(start, end - 1), which excludes the final valid index of the page. Every page therefore loses its last row, and the dropped rows are silently absent from render_page/summarize output. Concrete substitution with rows=["a","b","c","d","e"], page_size=2: page 0 -> start=0,end=2 -> range(0,1) -> ["a"] (drops "b"); page 1 -> start=2,end=4 -> range(2,3) -> ["c"] (drops "d"); page 2 -> start=4,end=5 -> range(4,4) -> [] (drops "e"). With page_size=1 every page renders empty. The _window_bounds docstring still promises half-open [start, end) bounds, so the loop contradicts its own contract.

findings.title: page_window drops the last row of every page (off-by-one)

Substituting rows=[1,2,3,4,5], page_size=2: page 0 -> range(0,1)=[1] (expected [1,2]); page 1 -> range(2,3)=[3] (expected [3,4]); page 2 -> range(4,4)=[] (expected [5]). This is a regression versus base, where the loop was `range(start, end)`.

findings.title: TtlCache.get inverted TTL check returns stale and evicts fresh
findings.whyItBreaks: The condition was flipped from `Date.now() - entry.storedAt < this.ttlMs` to `> this.ttlMs`. A fresh entry (age < ttlMs) now fails the check and falls through to `this.entries.delete(key); return null;`, so valid cached values are deleted and reported as misses, while an expired entry (age > ttlMs) now satisfies the check and is returned as if fresh. Caching is fully inverted: hits become misses and stale values are served as live.

findings.title: pruneDone skips consecutive done jobs via splice during forEach
findings.whyItBreaks: `jobs.splice(index, 1)` removes an element while `forEach` continues iterating by internal index. After removing element i, the next element shifts into index i and is skipped, so two adjacent done jobs leave the second one in the result. `pruneDone([{done:true},{done:true}])` returns an array still containing a done job, violating the function's contract.

findings.title: Inverted TTL check serves expired entries and drops fresh ones
findings.whyItBreaks: The TTL comparison was flipped from `<` to `>`. Now an entry whose age is GREATER than ttlMs is returned as valid (stale data served indefinitely), while an entry still within its TTL (age <= ttlMs) hits the else branch, is deleted, and returns null. Every fresh cache lookup now misses and evicts, and every expired entry is served as a hit — the exact inverse of TTL semantics. Base version returned fresh values and evicted expired ones.

findings.title: pruneDone skips consecutive done jobs and mutates caller array
findings.whyItBreaks: Replacing `filter` with an in-place `forEach` + `splice` is wrong twice. (1) Splicing during forEach shifts the next element into the current index while the iterator advances past it, so adjacent done jobs are skipped: input [done, done] yields [done] instead of []. (2) It mutates the caller's array in place, whereas the original returned a new array, so callers relying on the previous non-mutating contract see their input silently altered. The name/return type still promise a fully-pruned array.

findings.title: busiest mutates caller's array by sorting in place
findings.whyItBreaks: The old body copied the input (`[...rows].sort(...)`); the new body calls `rows.sort(...)` directly, reordering the caller's array as a side effect. Any caller that relies on the original order of `rows` (or shares/freezes the array) is silently corrupted after calling `busiest`. This is an in-place mutation of caller data introduced by this change.

findings.title: averageAmount returns NaN for empty rows after guard removal
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;` makes empty input evaluate `0 / 0`, returning NaN instead of the previous 0. NaN silently propagates through any arithmetic/summary/display built on this exported helper, whereas the prior contract returned a usable default.

findings.title: Restore empty-input guard in averageAmount to avoid NaN
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;` guard made empty input a defined 0. Now `total / rows.length` evaluates 0/0 → NaN for an empty array, so any consumer that formats, sums, or compares the average silently propagates NaN instead of 0, a behavior regression versus base.

findings.title: Avoid in-place sort mutation of caller array in busiest
findings.whyItBreaks: Base copied the array (`[...rows].sort(...)`); the new body calls `rows.sort(...)`, which reorders the caller's own array as a side effect. Callers that reuse the passed rows for display, pagination, or further iteration now see their data silently reordered after calling busiest, a regression in observable behavior.

findings.title: averageAmount([]) now returns NaN instead of 0
findings.whyItBreaks: The empty-array guard (`if (rows.length === 0) return 0;`) was removed, so for an empty input `total` is 0 and `0 / rows.length` is `0 / 0 === NaN`. This changes the exported function's established contract from `averageAmount([]) === 0` to `NaN`. Because NaN is a `number`, it silently propagates through callers' sums, averages, and comparisons (every comparison against NaN is false) rather than raising, so consumers render/propagate a wrong value instead of an error.

findings.title: busiest mutates the caller's array in place
findings.whyItBreaks: `rows.sort(...)` sorts the caller's array in place, replacing the prior defensive copy `[...rows].sort(...)`. Array.prototype.sort is mutating, so every caller's array is now reordered descending by amount as a side effect of a read-only query. Callers that rely on their original order (e.g. later iteration, indexing, or a second `busiest` call expecting stable input) observe corrupted order; this is an unintended in-place mutation of caller-owned data.

findings.title: Restore numeric ordering in rankScores (lexicographic sort regression)
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code used `scores.sort((a, b) => b - a)` (numeric descending). The new `rankScores` uses `scores.sort()` with no comparator, which coerces numbers to strings and orders them by UTF-16 code units, then reverses. For any scores with different digit counts the resulting order is not numeric descending, so the cutoff computed in topPlayers (line 15) is wrong and the returned top-N is wrong. Substitution: players=[{name:'A',score:3},{name:'B',score:100},{name:'C',score:20}], n=1 → scores.sort() = [100,20,3] → reverse = [3,20,100] → cutoff = scores[0] = 3 → filter score>=3 keeps all → slice(0,1) = [{score:3}]. Correct result is the score-100 player; head returns the score-3 player. Negative/decimal scores break similarly.

findings.title: rankScores sorts numerically as strings, breaking topPlayers cutoff
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort() with no comparator converts numbers to strings and orders them by UTF-16 code units, so score order is wrong whenever magnitudes differ in digit length (e.g. 9 vs 100 sorts as "100" < "9", reverse gives [9,100]). topPlayers derives its cutoff from this list: for players=[{name:'nine',score:9},{name:'hundred',score:100}], n=1, rankScores returns [9,100], cutoff=scores[0]=9, the filter keeps both, and slice(0,1) returns the score-9 player instead of the top score-100 player. The base version used (a,b)=>b-a and returned the correct top player. formatBoard inherits the same wrong output.

findings.title: Restore numeric comparator: comparator-less sort ranks scores lexicographically
findings.whyItBreaks: `Array.prototype.sort()` with no comparator converts elements to strings and orders them by UTF-16 code units, so `scores.sort(); scores.reverse()` yields descending *lexicographic* order, not descending numeric order. `topPlayers` then reads `cutoff = scores[Math.min(n, scores.length) - 1]` (src/leaderboard.ts:15) from this mis-ordered array and filters `p.score >= cutoff` (src/leaderboard.ts:16). Substituting real values: players=[{name:'a',score:50},{name:'b',score:100}], n=1. Old code: scores=[50,100] -> sort((a,b)=>b-a) -> [100,50] -> cutoff=scores[0]=100 -> filter >=100 -> [{b,100}] -> correct. New code: scores=[50,100] -> sort() -> ['100','50'] -> [100,50] -> reverse() -> [50,100] -> cutoff=scores[0]=50 -> filter >=50 keeps both in original order -> slice(0,1) -> [{a,50}]. The leaderboard returns the 50-point player instead of the 100-point player; formatBoard (src/leaderboard.ts:20) surfaces this wrong ranking to users.

findings.title: Restore constant-time comparison in signature verify()
findings.whyItBreaks: verify() previously used hmac.compare_digest(expected, given_signature), which compares in constant time. Replacing it with == makes the comparison short-circuit on the first differing byte, so the time to return varies with the number of matching leading characters of the attacker-supplied signature. An attacker can measure this timing (e.g. over the network or via repeated local calls) to recover the expected HMAC byte-by-byte and forge a valid signature, causing handle() at app/webhook.py:14 to return 200 and invoke processor(payload) for unauthenticated requests. This is a security regression, not a style change.

findings.title: Restore constant-time HMAC comparison in verify()
findings.whyItBreaks: verify() now compares the expected HMAC against the attacker-supplied signature with Python's `==`, which short-circuits on the first differing byte. The base revision used hmac.compare_digest, whose whole purpose is to run in time independent of where the strings differ. Because verify() gates the 401/200 decision in handle() (app/webhook.py:14), an unauthenticated caller can iteratively guess the signature byte-by-byte from response-timing differences and eventually forge a valid signature, defeating webhook authentication.

findings.title: Restore constant-time HMAC comparison in verify()
findings.whyItBreaks: verify() authenticates inbound webhooks and is the sole gate in handle() (app/webhook.py:14). Replacing hmac.compare_digest with the short-circuiting `==` on hex-digest strings makes the comparison time data-dependent: Python's str equality returns as soon as a differing character is found, so an attacker can recover the expected digest byte-by-byte by measuring response latency and forge a valid signature, bypassing the 401 rejection at app/webhook.py:14-15. The base revision correctly used hmac.compare_digest, so this is a security regression introduced by this diff.

findings.title: Keep balance updates inside the transfer transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this PR all three writes (ledger INSERT + both balance UPDATEs) ran inside `with db.transaction():`, so a failure anywhere rolled the whole transfer back. The refactor now commits `_record_ledger` inside the transaction at line 23, then calls `_apply_balances` at line 24 OUTSIDE the transaction. The debit and credit UPDATEs are no longer covered by that transaction, so they either autocommit individually or are never committed, depending on the db wrapper. In either case the transfer is no longer atomic: if the credit UPDATE (or the process) fails after the debit is applied, the ledger records a completed transfer while funds are debited but never credited (or the ledger row is committed with no balance change at all). This is a data-integrity/data-loss regression on the money-movement path, and the return `{"ok": True}` still reports success.

findings.title: Balance updates run outside the transfer transaction, breaking atomicity
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change all three statements (ledger INSERT, debit UPDATE, credit UPDATE) executed inside `with db.transaction():`. Now only `_record_ledger` runs inside the transaction; `_apply_balances` (the two UPDATEs) runs after the `with` block exits, i.e. after the ledger INSERT has been committed. If either UPDATE fails (or the process dies between commit and updates), the ledger permanently records the transfer while account balances are never debited/credited, and if the second UPDATE fails the first debit is also left committed un-credited. The previous single-transaction behavior rolled all three back together, so this is a real data-integrity regression on the live `transfer` path.

findings.title: Restore atomic transaction around ledger and balance writes
findings.whyItBreaks: In the base version the ledger INSERT and both balance UPDATEs ran inside a single `with db.transaction():` block, so they committed or rolled back together. This PR moved the two UPDATEs into `_apply_balances` and calls it at line 24, AFTER the `with db.transaction():` block has exited. The ledger INSERT is now committed in its own transaction while the debit/credit run outside any transaction. If the debit succeeds and the credit fails (constraint error, connection drop, process crash), the ledger records a completed transfer and the source account is debited without the destination being credited — a non-atomic money movement that loses funds and desyncs ledger vs. balances. A concurrent reader can also observe the ledger entry with no matching balance change.

findings.title: billingDay now uses local time instead of UTC, shifting day boundaries
findings.whyItBreaks: Before, billingDay derived the day from getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate, so the result was a stable UTC calendar day regardless of where the process ran. The new body uses getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, which read the host's local timezone. The same instant now maps to different billing days on hosts in different zones (e.g. 2026-03-01T00:30Z is '2026-03-01' under UTC but '2026-02-28' on a UTC-5 host), and sameBillingDay compares two dates using these local-derived strings. For a billing boundary this shifts charge/period attribution by up to a day depending on deployment TZ and can make two hosts disagree, producing incorrect billing-day classification.

findings.title: billingDay now uses local time, breaking UTC-stable billing day
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation derived the day from getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate, so a given instant mapped to exactly one billing day regardless of host timezone. The new body reads getFullYear()/getMonth()/getDate(), which return the host-local calendar values. For any server running with TZ != UTC the returned string changes (e.g. 2026-03-01T02:00:00Z becomes '2026-03-01' under UTC but '2026-02-28' under America/Los_Angeles), so the same instant is classified into different billing days depending on the deployment environment. sameBillingDay (src/billing/day.ts:8) inherits the same defect and can now report two instants as different days (or vice versa) based purely on the process timezone. This is a behavioral regression to an exported/public function whose output feeds billing classification.

findings.title: billingDay now derives from local time, breaking UTC billing boundaries
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation used getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate, so the billing day was a stable function of the instant. The new line uses getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, which read the process's local timezone. For any non-UTC host the same instant now maps to a different billing day, and instants near local-vs-UTC midnight (e.g. 2026-01-01T00:30Z on a UTC+8 host) shift by one day. Because sameBillingDay (line 8) delegates to billingDay, both the day key and the equality predicate inherit the host-timezone dependency, so billing classification changes with server TZ rather than with the timestamp — a user-visible regression for billing windows.

findings.title: Cache key drops tenant, causing cross-tenant profile collision
findings.whyItBreaks: `memo` is a single module-level Map shared across all tenants (src/profile.ts:7). The cache key was `${tenant}:${account}` and is now just `account`. `fetchProfile(tenant, account)` results depend on both tenant and account, so tenant A/account "alice" and tenant B/account "alice" now map to the same slot. After A populates it, B's readProfile hits `if (cached) return cached` (src/profile.ts:15-16) and returns A's Profile object instead of calling fetchProfile — a cross-tenant data-isolation break and wrong-profile return. The same collision also makes the second tenant's `memo.set(key, profile)` (src/profile.ts:18) overwrite the first tenant's entry.

findings.title: Restore tenant scoping in memo cache key to prevent cross-tenant profile leakage
findings.whyItBreaks: `memo` (src/profile.ts:7) is a module-level Map shared across all callers. Keying it only by `account` (was `${tenant}:${account}`) means readProfile('tenantA','bob',...) stores under key 'bob', and a later readProfile('tenantB','bob',...) hits the cached branch at src/profile.ts:16 and returns tenantA's Profile without ever calling fetchProfile. Two distinct tenants sharing an account name now receive each other's profile — a tenant-isolation/data-disclosure regression introduced by this change.

findings.title: Restore tenant in memo cache key to prevent cross-tenant collision
findings.whyItBreaks: The cache key changed from `${tenant}:${account}` to `account`, so the module-level `memo` Map (src/profile.ts:7) is now keyed only by account name. Two different tenants that share an account name collide: after `readProfile('tenantA', 'alice', ...)` populates the cache, a later `readProfile('tenantB', 'alice', ...)` hits `memo.get('alice')` at src/profile.ts:15 and returns tenantA's cached Profile without ever calling `fetchProfile`, leaking/returning the wrong tenant's profile data (including displayName and the Profile.tenant/account fields). The fetch path at src/profile.ts:17 is skipped entirely for the colliding tenant.

findings.title: load() swallows missing-key error into indistinguishable empty string
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously `load` threw `Error('missing: key')`, so a failed lookup propagated as a hard failure. The new catch-all replaces any failure with `""`, but `""` is a valid `Map<string, string>` value, so callers cannot tell 'key absent' from 'key present with empty value'. The public `load`/`loadAll` contract now forces every caller to conflate a missing key with real data and act on it (persist/report/route as if valid).

findings.title: Don't swallow missing-key error in load(); it hides failures as ""
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously load() threw `missing: ${key}` when a key was absent, so callers could distinguish a missing entry from a stored value. The new catch-all converts every failure (including the explicit `missing:` throw, and any future error thrown inside store.get) into "". loadAll() propagates this directly (keys.map -> load), so a returned "" is now ambiguous: it can mean a genuinely-empty stored value or a key that was never present. Any caller that persists, bills, or reports on the returned value will treat the failure as real data. This is an exported public API, so the unusable contract is a present defect regardless of in-repo callers.

findings.title: Stop swallowing load()'s missing-key error into an empty string
findings.whyItBreaks: TRIGGER D (swallowed failure). Before this change load() threw Error(`missing: ${key}`) when a key was absent; the new try/catch catches that throw (and any other error) and returns "" instead. The failure signal is now indistinguishable from a legitimately stored empty value at every call site. The in-repo consumer loadAll (src/store.ts:12) maps load over keys, so a batch containing a missing key silently yields an empty-string slot instead of aborting; any caller that persists, displays, or branches on that result will treat a missing entry as real data. This is an exported/public API (src/store.ts:1), so the contract itself is now unusable: every eventual caller is forced to conflate "missing" with a real "" value.

findings.title: retryBackground silently swallows every failure
findings.whyItBreaks: retryBackground is a newly added exported function whose only failure channel is discarded: `catch { continue; }` at src/retry.ts:27 drops the error and the function returns void after all attempts are exhausted, with no rethrow, return value, or log. A caller therefore cannot distinguish a fully-failed background task from a successful one, so it may proceed as if the work succeeded.

findings.title: Config rename timeoutMs->timeout breaks existing callers
findings.whyItBreaks: Config is exported. Renaming timeoutMs to timeout and adding a required retries field breaks existing callers: TypeScript consumers fail to compile, and untyped/stale callers passing the old shape {maxAttempts, timeoutMs} get config.timeout === undefined, so deadline = Date.now() + undefined = NaN at src/retry.ts:8 and `Date.now() > NaN` is false at src/retry.ts:10 - the deadline guard never fires and the timeout is silently not enforced. For retryBackground, config.retries === undefined makes the loop at src/retry.ts:22 run zero iterations, a silent no-op.

findings.title: Renaming exported Config.timeoutMs to timeout breaks callers and drops unit
findings.whyItBreaks: `Config` is the exported public contract of this module. Renaming `timeoutMs` to `timeout` (and adding a new required `retries` field) is a breaking change: existing consumers that construct `{ maxAttempts, timeoutMs }` no longer satisfy the type, and untyped callers still passing `timeoutMs` get `config.timeout === undefined` at src/retry.ts:8, so `deadline = Date.now() + undefined = NaN` and the guard `Date.now() > deadline` (src/retry.ts:10) is always false — the deadline is silently never enforced and the loop runs the full attempt count. The rename also removes the explicit millisecond unit, inviting callers to pass seconds.

findings.title: Renamed Config.timeout silently disables the retry deadline
findings.whyItBreaks: Config is exported and its required field was renamed timeoutMs→timeout. A caller that still passes { maxAttempts, timeoutMs } yields config.timeout === undefined; Date.now() + undefined is NaN, and the guard `Date.now() > deadline` at src/retry.ts:10 (and :23) is false for NaN, so the deadline check never fires and the loop always runs the full attempt count. The timeout is silently ignored instead of erroring, for both retry and retryBackground. The old name also encoded units (ms); the new unitless `timeout` no longer states them although the body treats it as ms.

findings.title: Field accepts number but value.length yields undefined for numeric input
findings.whyItBreaks: Line 2 widens the public FieldProps.value to `string | number`, but line 6 computes `len=${value.length}`. `number` has no `length` property, so this is a TypeScript error (TS2339: Property 'length' does not exist on type 'string | number') that breaks typecheck/build for this exported component. At runtime, a numeric value makes `value.length` evaluate to `undefined`, producing the label `len=undefined`; the previous behavior of rendering the value via `defaultValue={value}` is also gone, so a numeric consumer gets a meaningless string instead of any representation of the value. The type annotation promises numbers are accepted while the body implements none of that handling (Trigger C: promise != implementation on an exported carrier).

findings.title: Handle numeric value in Field instead of calling .length
findings.whyItBreaks: The interface now advertises `value: string | number`, but the body computes `value.length`. For a numeric value `5`, `(5).length` is `undefined`, so `label` becomes the string "len=undefined" and the input's defaultValue is that wrong literal rather than a length derived from the value. The widened public type promises number support the body does not implement, and under TypeScript the union itself fails to typecheck (`Property 'length' does not exist on type 'string | number'`).

findings.title: Field no longer renders its value; shows a length label instead
findings.whyItBreaks: Base behavior passed the supplied value straight to the input (`defaultValue={value}`). The change replaces that with `defaultValue={label}`, so the input now displays `len=<n>` rather than the value it was given. Every caller that relied on Field displaying its value now shows a wrong string, an observable user-facing regression on the component's core behavior.

findings.title: Number values produce len=undefined; type widening contradicts body
findings.whyItBreaks: Line 2 widens the exported contract to `value: string | number`, promising numbers are accepted, but line 6 computes `value.length`. `Number` has no `length`, so a numeric value yields `undefined` and the label becomes `len=undefined`; under TypeScript this is a compile error (`Property 'length' does not exist on type 'string | number'`), so the declared number support is not implemented and the module fails to type-check.

findings.title: Remove step that echoes secret TOKEN into workflow logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The added step injects `secrets.TOKEN` into the shell and prints it with `echo "deploying with $TOKEN"`, writing the credential into the job log. This job runs on every `on: push` event (deploy.yml:2), so the secret is emitted on each push. Log-based secret masking is best-effort and bypassable (transformations, partial output, log-forwarding to third-party collectors, artifact/archive of raw logs), so this is a credential-exposure surface with no functional benefit. It also needlessly expands the secret's blast radius to any actor who can read workflow logs.

findings.title: Remove step that echoes secret TOKEN into build logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The added step injects secrets.TOKEN into the environment and writes it to stdout (`echo "deploying with $TOKEN"`). Workflow logs are retained and visible to anyone with read access to Actions logs, and GitHub's log masking is best-effort and bypassable (transformed/partial output, ANSI sequences), so this deliberately leaks a live credential. The step also does not deploy anything, so the only effect of the change is credential exposure.

findings.title: Stop echoing repository secret into workflow logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The new step injects `secrets.TOKEN` into the environment and immediately `echo`s it, writing the credential to the Actions log. Log masking is best-effort only: it fails when the value is transformed, split, or emitted by a tool, and logs are broadly readable (anyone with repo/log access, plus log-export/CI integrations). The workflow triggers on `on: push`, so the secret is emitted on every push. This step also performs no deploy work — it only leaks the token.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer on git() so large PR diffs don't abort review
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer makes spawnSync fall back to Node's default of 1024*1024 (1 MiB). Verified locally on node v24: a 2 MiB stdout yields res.error.code='ENOBUFS', res.status=null and truncated stdout. git() is the capture path for the full patch at line 140 (`git(["diff", mergeBase, headSha])`) and for changedFileSet at line 57; a real PR whose diff exceeds 1 MiB therefore hits ENOBUFS, the guard `res.status !== 0` sees null and throws `git diff ... failed: ` (empty stderr, since diff output goes to stdout), and runGithub's catch posts a failure check and exits 1. Previously the 64 MiB limit allowed large diffs. gh()/ghText() (lines 16-29) still keep 64 MiB, so only the git path regressed.

findings.title: Restore git maxBuffer: 1 MiB default aborts large-diff reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: The git() helper dropped `maxBuffer: 1024 * 1024 * 64`, so spawnSync falls back to Node's ~1 MiB default. `git diff mergeBase headSha` (line 140) can exceed that on a moderately large PR; spawnSync then sets res.error.code = ENOBUFS with status null, so `res.status !== 0` is true and git() throws (stderr empty) before review() ever runs. runGithub catches that and posts a failing check, aborting the review instead of reviewing the PR.

findings.title: Send merge-base, not live base tip, as bundle.baseSha
findings.whyItBreaks: The patch and changedFiles are computed from mergeBase (lines 140-141), but bundle.baseSha now carries the live PR base tip (`baseSha`, line 138). When the base branch has advanced past the fork point these differ, so the bundle is inconsistent: it declares a base commit that is not the base of the diff it contains. Any downstream consumer that trusts bundle.baseSha (re-diffing baseSha..headSha, or rendering the reviewed range) inspects a different range than what was actually reviewed — and the reviewed patch is still mergeBase..headSha, so this silently misreports the review scope.

findings.title: Restore git() maxBuffer to avoid ENOBUFS abort on large diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: Dropping maxBuffer falls back to Node's default of 1 MiB. The git() helper is used at line 140 to capture the full PR patch (git diff <mergeBase> <headSha>), which routinely exceeds 1 MiB (lockfiles, generated/vendored code). On overflow spawnSync returns status=null with error.code=ENOBUFS and signal=SIGTERM (verified: truncated at ~1,077,248 bytes). The guard `res.status !== 0` (line 38) treats null as failure and throws, and that call sits outside the try/catch (which begins at line 176), so runGithub rejects and no review is posted for any large PR. The sibling gh()/ghText() helpers still pass 64 MiB (lines 19, 29), confirming this removal is unintended.

findings.title: Restore `-s read-only` on codex exec to keep sandbox pinned
findings.whyItBreaks: `runCodex` spawns `codex exec` in the repo under review and pipes the review prompt (untrusted PR content) to it via stdin. Previously the args hard-coded `-s read-only`, so even if the user config (`~/.codex/config.toml`) or a trusted project `.codex/config.toml` set a looser policy, the CLI override won. Removing the flag means `sandbox_mode_override` is now `None` (codex-rs/exec/src/lib.rs sets `sandbox_mode` only when `-s` is passed) and the sandbox is resolved from config: for a git repo with a trust decision the default is `workspace-write` (codex-rs/config/src/config_toml.rs `derive_permission_profile` falls back to `SandboxMode::WorkspaceWrite` when `active_project.is_trusted() || is_untrusted()`), and any configured `sandbox_mode` (workspace-write / danger-full-access) now takes effect. That turns a read-only reviewer into an agent that can write to the repo under review and run commands without approvals (exec forces `approval_policy: Never`), so injected instructions in the reviewed diff gain a filesystem/exec surface that was previously denied.

findings.title: Pin read-only sandbox for codex exec on untrusted reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: `runCodex` spawns `codex exec` with `cwd: opts.repoPath` (line 24), i.e. it runs the agent directly over the repository under review, whose PR content is untrusted. The deleted `-s read-only` was the highest-precedence source for the sandbox mode: codex resolves `sandbox_mode` from config layers when no CLI `-s` is given (user `~/.codex/config.toml`, plus the project's `.codex/config.toml` for trusted projects). If any layer sets `sandbox_mode = "workspace-write"|"danger-full-access"` or `default_permissions = ":danger-full-access"`, this review subprocess now executes the untrusted repo with write/full access instead of read-only; the CLI flag previously overrode such config and pinned read-only. Note: `codex exec`'s built-in default is still read-only, so the regression is silent until a config layer differs — the change removes the guarantee rather than the default.

findings.title: Restore explicit read-only sandbox on codex exec invocation
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff deletes `-s read-only` from the `codex exec` args. Previously the function hard-forced the read-only sandbox; now the effective sandbox falls back to ambient configuration (`~/.codex/config.toml` `sandbox_mode`/`default_permissions`, or `[projects."<path>"] trust_level`, which resolves to the `:workspace` profile for trusted/untrusted projects — see codex-rs `default_builtin_permission_profile_name`). `codex exec` always forces `approval_policy = Never`, so there is no approval gate to catch writes. Because `runCodex` feeds untrusted reviewed-repo content as the prompt with `cwd = opts.repoPath`, any environment where the default resolves to `workspace-write` now lets the reviewing sub-agent modify/execute inside the checkout under review. The flag was harmless under the default config, so removing it only drops a defense-in-depth guarantee with no functional upside.

findings.title: Restore merge-base: diff now includes base-branch-only changes
findings.whyItBreaks: In CI, PR_BASE_SHA is the base branch tip (e.g. main at event time), not the fork point once main advances after the PR branched. `git diff baseSha HEAD` is a two-dot diff, so every commit merged into base since the fork is rendered as reverse hunks: the reviewed patch gains phantom deletions and `changedPaths` (built from `changedFileSet` at line 57, which also diffs baseSha..HEAD) lists files the PR never touched, which then gates inline-comment placement at src/adapters/github.ts:73/141. The removed `merge-base baseSha headSha` previously restricted both the patch and the file set to the PR's own commits.

findings.title: Restore merge-base so PR diff excludes unrelated base-branch changes
findings.whyItBreaks: baseSha is either PR_BASE_SHA (the base branch tip on a GitHub Actions pull_request event, i.e. github.event.pull_request.base.sha) or merge-base(origin/main, HEAD). The removed line normalized it with `git merge-base baseSha headSha`, so the old `git diff mergeBase headSha` always diffed from the fork point. The new two-dot `git diff baseSha HEAD` diffs the base tip directly against HEAD: if the base branch has advanced past the fork point, every commit merged to base after the fork appears inverted (as deletions) in the patch and in `--name-only`, so the model reviews/classifies files this PR never touched. That polluted set also feeds changedPaths, and inlineComments()'s filter `changedPaths.has(f.file)` at src/adapters/github.ts:63 then allows inline comments for lines that are not part of the PR's diff; the GitHub reviews API rejects those (422), the empty catch at src/adapters/github.ts:96 silently swallows it, and the fallback re-posts the review with `comments` omitted, dropping every inline finding. Secondary: the diff now uses the literal `HEAD` instead of headSha, so when PR_HEAD_SHA differs from the checked-out commit the patch is computed for a different commit than the `commit_id: headSha` sent at src/adapters/github.ts:85.

findings.title: Restore merge-base so the reviewed diff is the PR's own changes
findings.whyItBreaks: baseSha is the base branch tip (PR_BASE_SHA) while HEAD is the checked-out PR head, so `git diff baseSha HEAD` is a two-dot diff against the current base tip. When the base branch has advanced past the PR's branch point (the common, un-rebased case), this diff includes the reverse of every commit merged into base since the branch point plus every file those commits touched. Previously `merge-base(baseSha, headSha)` restricted the diff to the PR's own changes (three-dot semantics). As a result `patch` fed to the reviewer and `changedPaths` derived from `changedFileSet(cwd, baseSha)` now contain files/lines the PR never modified: the reviewer can flag unrelated code, miss the real change, and `inlineComments` may try to post comments on files not in the PR diff.

findings.title: Restore function-form replace callbacks to avoid $ substitution
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace only treats the replacement literally when it is a function; when it is a string, JS interprets special patterns `$$`, `$&`, `` $` `` and `$'`. The previous code used `() => ...` precisely to bypass that. Now `JSON.stringify(bundle, null, 2)` (which embeds `bundle.patch` and any source text) and `bundle.patch` itself are inserted as raw replacement strings, so any `$`-sequence in a reviewed diff (e.g. `$$` in shell/Makefile, `$'` in bash/PowerShell, `$&`) is rewritten: `$$` collapses to `$`, `$&`/`` $` ``/`$'` inject the matched placeholder or surrounding prompt text. The model then reviews a corrupted patch/bundle with no error raised, producing wrong review results.

findings.title: Restore function replacers so $ patterns aren't expanded in prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: Passing a plain string as `replace()`'s second argument makes JS interpret `$$`, `$&`, `` $` `` and `$'` as special replacement patterns; previously the `() => …` replacers returned the text verbatim (see base `git show 94bd7b9:src/core/review.ts:25,32-33`). Now `JSON.stringify(bundle)` (line 25), `JSON.stringify(candidate)` (line 32) and especially the raw `bundle.patch` (line 33) get `$` sequences rewritten before reaching the critic model: a diff line containing `$&` is replaced by the literal match `{{PATCH}}`, `$$` collapses to `$`, and `` $` ``/`$'` splice surrounding template text into the prompt. The critic then reviews corrupted code/prompt, silently changing the verdict — the exact failure the base code avoided. `$` sequences (`$&` in JS `replace` code, `$$` in shell/Make, `$'` in bash) are common in real diffs.

findings.title: Keep replacer functions: string replacement mangles $ sequences in bundle/patch
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace treats `$` sequences in a *string* replacement as substitution patterns: `$$` -> `$`, `$&` -> the matched placeholder (`{{BUNDLE}}`/`{{FINDINGS}}`/`{{PATCH}}`), and `$` + backtick / `$'` -> the entire prompt text before/after the match. The base code passed `() => ...` replacer functions, which return the value literally and are immune to this. The head passes `JSON.stringify(bundle, null, 2)`, `JSON.stringify(candidate, null, 2)`, and `bundle.patch` directly, so any `$`-sequence in the reviewed diff or findings (e.g. `$$` in shell/PHP/Make text, `$&` in JS `.replace` code, `$'` ANSI-C quoting) silently drops characters or splices large chunks of the prompt template into the wrong place, corrupting the exact artifact under review. Verified semantics: `'A{{P}}B'.replace('{{P}}','$$')` -> 'A$B', `$&` -> 'A{{P}}B', 'x$`y' -> 'AxAyB', "x$'y" -> 'AxByB'.

findings.title: Keep commit_id in the review retry so it targets the reviewed SHA
findings.whyItBreaks: postReview's primary payload still pins the review to headSha (line 89), but this diff removes `-f commit_id=${headSha}` from the catch fallback (lines 100-112), so the retry is created without commit_id. GitHub then applies its default and attaches the review to the PR's current head rather than headSha, the SHA the diff, verdict and inline anchors were computed from (headSha is resolved at line 141 and passed to postReview/postCheck at lines 183-184). If the branch advanced while the review ran (reviews take minutes), the fallback posts REQUEST_CHANGES/COMMENT as if the newest commit had been reviewed while postCheck still binds the check-run to headSha, so the two posts disagree about which commit was reviewed and the verdict is attributed to unanalyzed code.

findings.title: Restore commit_id pin in fallback review POST
findings.whyItBreaks: The fallback POST to repos/{repo}/pulls/{n}/reviews no longer sends commit_id, and the GitHub API defaults commit_id to the PR's most recent commit. The primary payload (line 89) still pins commit_id=headSha, so the two paths now disagree: when the inline-comment request fails and the head has advanced past the SHA that was actually reviewed, the fallback files the verdict (including REQUEST_CHANGES) against a commit this tool never analyzed, and the posted review is no longer associated with the SHA it evaluated.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of silently defaulting them
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding previously threw on every malformed field; it now substitutes defaults: an unknown/invalid severity becomes "P1", an invalid category becomes "bug", a missing file becomes "" (line 103), missing title becomes "Untitled finding" (line 99), missing whyItBreaks/suggestedFix become "" (lines 107-108), and lineStart/lineEnd become 0 or NaN for non-numeric input (lines 104-105). Because the function is exported, every caller is forced to conflate malformed model output with a legitimate finding: a bogus severity is silently inflated to P1, and a finding with file="" and lineStart=0 is emitted as if it anchored to a real location, so consumers cannot detect or reject it.

findings.title: Removed strict path discards the malformed-review error signal
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview dropped its `strict = true` parameter (line 113) and the branch that rejected/propagated malformed findings, leaving only `raw.findings.map(normalizeFinding)` (line 131). Previously a default call `normalizeReview(raw)` threw on any malformed finding and `normalizeReview(raw, false)` filtered them out; now both silently pass coerced findings through. The exported signature no longer offers any mode that surfaces the failure, so callers who relied on the strict default to detect bad model output receive plausible-looking findings instead of an error.

findings.title: Stop coercing malformed findings into fabricated defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: The old normalizeFinding threw on every invalid field (severity, category, file, title, whyItBreaks, suggestedFix, lineStart, lineEnd), and normalizeReview(strict=false) caught and DROPPED those findings while strict=true aborted the review. The new body defaults each field instead: invalid severity -> "P1" (line 98), invalid category -> "bug" (100-102), missing file -> "" (103), missing lines -> 0/0 (104-105), missing title -> "Untitled finding" (99), empty whyItBreaks/suggestedFix (107-108). The exported/public swallow site therefore maps failure to a real-looking value, so a downstream consumer cannot tell a malformed finding from a genuine P1/bug finding with file "" and range 0-0; it may emit or act on fabricated findings. Removing the `strict` parameter (line 113) also deletes the only way callers could request the old drop/abort semantics, and an invalid `lineEnd` now yields NaN instead of throwing (105).

findings.title: Malformed findings silently coerced to defaults instead of rejected
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change normalizeFinding threw on every malformed field (invalid/missing severity, category, file, title, whyItBreaks, suggestedFix, lineStart/lineEnd <= 0), so a bad finding propagated as an error (normalizeReview strict=true) or was dropped (strict=false). Now the function never rejects an object-shaped input: an unknown severity becomes a real "P1" (line 98), an unknown category becomes "bug" (lines 100-102), and a missing file/lineStart/whyItBreaks becomes ""/0 (lines 103-104, 107), producing a Finding that is structurally valid and indistinguishable from a genuine result. A hallucinated or truncated finding is therefore surfaced to the consumer as a real P1 bug finding rather than being flagged/dropped, and the strict/non-strict distinction (and its ability to fail closed) is gone because normalizeReview's `strict` parameter was also removed (line 113, 131). The defaulting is the swallow: failure is mapped to a legitimate-looking value, so callers acting on it persist/report a fabricated finding as real.

findings.title: Restore -R in gh pr view; repo unresolvable before checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The `Resolve PR refs` step executes BEFORE `actions/checkout` (line 42), so at that moment there is no git repository in the working directory. `gh` resolves the target repo only from `-R/--repo`, `GH_REPO`, or a git remote; it does NOT read `GITHUB_REPOSITORY` (verified: 0 occurrences in gh 2.98.0). The diff removed both the `REPO` env var and `-R "$REPO"`, leaving neither. On a cold workspace (first run on a self-hosted runner, or any cleaned workspace) the command fails with `failed to run git: fatal: not a git repository`, and because it is wrapped in `echo "head=$(...)" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"` under the default `bash -e`, the failure is swallowed and the step succeeds writing empty `head=`/`base=` (verified: `bash -e -c 'echo "head=$(false)"'` exits 0). Downstream, `steps.refs.outputs.head` (line 45) becomes empty so `actions/checkout` falls back to the dispatch branch instead of the requested PR head, and `PR_BASE_SHA`/`PR_HEAD_SHA` (lines 56-57) are empty — the manual workflow_dispatch review silently runs against the wrong revision.

findings.title: Restore repo context for gh pr view in pre-checkout step
findings.whyItBreaks: These `gh pr view` calls run in the "Resolve PR refs" step, which is the FIRST step and executes before `actions/checkout` (line 42). Without a local git repository (or `GH_REPO`), gh cannot infer the target repo: `gh help environment` documents repo selection only via `-R/--repo` or `GH_REPO`, and GITHUB_REPOSITORY is not honored. The removed `-R "$REPO"` (plus the removed `REPO: ${{ github.repository }}` env at the former line 30) was the only thing supplying that context. On the workflow_dispatch path (EVENT_HEAD is empty, so the else branch runs), gh exits non-zero with a 'not a git repository / could not determine repo' error. Because the call is inside `$(...)` feeding `echo`, bash -e does not fail the step; the outputs are written empty, so `steps.refs.outputs.head`/`base` are blank, checkout falls back to the default ref, and the needlefish review runs with empty PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA (silent wrong refs rather than a loud failure).

findings.title: Restore -R repo flag in gh pr view (no checkout yet at this step)
findings.whyItBreaks: The `Resolve PR refs` step runs BEFORE the `Checkout PR head` step (actions/checkout is at line 43), so at execution time the runner workspace has no cloned git repository and thus no resolvable `origin` remote. `gh pr view` without `-R`/`GH_REPO` infers the target repo from the current git remote and fails when none exists ("not a git repository" / could not determine repo). The previous `-R "$REPO"` (with `REPO: ${{ github.repository }}`) supplied that context explicitly. This `else` branch is the only path taken for `workflow_dispatch`, so manual reviews now fail at step 1 with a non-zero exit; the `pull_request` path is unaffected because it uses EVENT_HEAD/EVENT_BASE and never reaches this branch.

findings.title: Don't drop candidate findings via non-strict normalizeReview
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview(raw, strict = true) uses the flag only to choose per-finding error handling: strict maps every finding through normalizeFinding (which throws on any malformed required field: invalid severity/category, lineEnd < lineStart, non-finite/negative line, confidence < 0.7 for P0-P2, missing whyItBreaks/suggestedFix), while non-strict wraps each in try/catch, converts the failure to null, and filters it out. Passing false on the candidate pass therefore silently deletes a candidate finding that has one malformed field instead of aborting. The only post-parse guard (src/core/review.ts:30) checks summary and checked, never findings, so it admits the truncated result; candidate is then serialized into the critic prompt (src/core/review.ts:35) and the final result takes findings exclusively from pruned (src/core/review.ts:48), with the critic restricted to pruning. A real P1/P2 finding the candidate emitted can thus disappear from the review, and deriveVerdict can return pass. Pre-change the same malformed output threw out of review(), keeping failure loud and distinguishable; the sibling critic call (src/core/review.ts:38) still uses the strict default, so the two passes normalize inconsistently.

findings.title: Candidate pass parsed with strict=false silently drops malformed findings
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview(raw, strict=false) catches normalizeFinding validation errors and filters those findings out instead of throwing (strict=true is the default and the behavior of the critic call on line 38). The candidate's findings are the only input the critic receives — line 35 substitutes JSON.stringify(candidate) into {{FINDINGS}} — and the final result's findings come solely from pruned.findings (line 48). So a genuine finding whose output has one malformed required field (e.g. blocking severity with confidence<0.7, lineEnd<lineStart, invalid severity/category) is silently removed from candidate.findings; the guard on line 30 checks only summary and checked, not findings, so an empty findings list passes and the run can emit pass on a PR that really has a P1/P2 defect. Before this change the malformed finding raised and aborted the pass instead of disappearing.

findings.title: normalizeReview silently swallows malformed review output as an empty review
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously normalizeReview threw for a non-object payload and for missing/non-string summary, missing/non-array findings, checked, or residual_risks (base lines 115-129). The new body defaults every missing or wrong-typed field instead: findings->[], checked->[], residual_risks->[], summary->"". So any malformed response (null, undefined, a truncated JSON object missing findings, a string) is now returned as {summary:"", findings:[], checked:[], residual_risks:[]} — a value indistinguishable from a genuine clean review. An exported/public path that maps failure to a default value is the defect itself: every caller is forced to conflate a failed review with a legitimate 'no findings, no risks' result, which downstream verdict logic would treat as pass instead of surfacing a retry/failure.

findings.title: Restore hard failure for malformed review output
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation threw for every malformed shape: non-object input, non-string `summary`, and non-array `findings`/`checked`/`residual_risks` (`git show fe8a7f9:src/shared/schema.ts`). The new body coerces each of those to `[]`/`""` via `Array.isArray(...) ? ... : []` and `String(raw?.summary ?? "")`, so `null`, a string, `{}`, or `{findings: "oops"}` now all return `{summary: "", findings: [], checked: [], residual_risks: []}`. A crashed or unparseable reviewer response is therefore no longer distinguishable from a legitimate zero-finding review, and `residual_risks` is silently emptied so no `blocks` signal can be raised. This is an exported public function, so every caller is forced to conflate failure with a real value.

findings.title: normalizeReview swallows malformed review output into an empty review
findings.whyItBreaks: Every explicit guard that previously rejected malformed model output was deleted. Previously normalizeReview(null), a non-object, a missing/non-string summary, or missing findings/checked/residual_risks arrays threw a distinguishable Error ("malformed review output: ..."). Now each field is defaulted instead: findings→[] (L115-117), residual_risks→[] (L118-123), summary→"" (L125), checked→[] (L127), and even a non-object raw yields this same object because the `!raw || typeof raw !== "object"` guard is gone. The result is a structurally valid RawReview indistinguishable from a legitimate review that reported zero findings, so a caller that parses review output can no longer tell "the model produced garbage" from "the model approved with no findings" and may treat a failed/garbled review as a clean pass. This is an exported public contract, so the defect ships regardless of in-repo callers: every future caller is forced to conflate failure with a real value.

findings.title: Manual workflow_dispatch path no longer resolves PR head/base refs
findings.whyItBreaks: The workflow keeps `workflow_dispatch` with a required `pr_number` input (line 10-14) and the job `if` explicitly allows it (line 24), but the removed `Resolve PR refs` step was the only thing that populated head/base for that event. On workflow_dispatch there is no `github.event.pull_request` object, so `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` (line 46) and `github.event.pull_request.base.sha` (line 45) expand to empty strings, and `github.event.pull_request.base.ref || 'main'` (line 35) always becomes `main` instead of the PR's real base. The checkout ref `github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.ref` (line 29) therefore falls back to `github.ref` — the branch the dispatch was launched from, not the PR head commit. Result: the review runs against the wrong commit (and wrong base) for every manual dispatch, whereas the base version resolved them via `gh pr view`.

findings.title: workflow_dispatch no longer resolves PR head/base refs
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, github.event.pull_request is empty, so `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` is '' and the checkout falls back to `github.ref` (the branch the workflow was dispatched on, normally the default branch) instead of the PR head; `github.event.pull_request.base.ref` at line 35 falls back to 'main' even when the PR targets another branch; and PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA at lines 45-46 become empty strings. The deleted 'Resolve PR refs' step handled exactly this case via `gh pr view` (headRefOid/baseRefOid/baseRef), so the manual-trigger path that `on.workflow_dispatch` and the job `if` at line 24 explicitly support is regressed: it reviews the wrong revision with empty base/head SHAs.

findings.title: Manual dispatch path loses PR ref resolution (wrong checkout, empty SHAs)
findings.whyItBreaks: The workflow still supports `workflow_dispatch` with a required `pr_number` input (lines 10-14, and the `if:` on line 24 explicitly allows `github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch'`), but the diff deleted the `Resolve PR refs` step that used `gh pr view "$PR_NUM" --json headRefOid/baseRefOid/baseRef` for the non-pull_request case. On workflow_dispatch there is no `github.event.pull_request` payload, so: (1) line 29 `ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.ref }}` falls back to `github.ref`, i.e. the branch the workflow was dispatched from (normally the default branch) instead of the PR head — the tool then reviews the wrong working tree; (2) line 35 `BASE_REF` falls back to 'main' rather than the PR's real base branch; (3) lines 45-46 resolve `PR_BASE_SHA`/`PR_HEAD_SHA` to empty strings, so the CLI invoked on line 47 receives no diff range. Previously all three values were resolved from the PR number via `gh pr view`, so the manual-trigger feature worked.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer: 1 MiB default breaks git diff on large PRs
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync's default maxBuffer is 1 MiB (1024*1024). The git() helper is used to capture the full patch via git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"], cwd) at src/adapters/local.ts:100, and also merge-base/rev-parse/name-only. When stdout exceeds maxBuffer, Node kills the child, sets res.error=ENOBUFS with res.status=null and res.stderr=null, so the guard at line 12 throws `git diff <base> HEAD failed: ` (empty stderr) and runLocal aborts before any review. Previously maxBuffer was 64 MiB, so PRs with large diffs (lockfiles, generated files, vendored code) reviewed fine; now they hard-fail. The sibling gh() helper at line 36 still sets 64 MiB, confirming the intended bound.

findings.title: Restore git() maxBuffer so large diffs don't abort the review
findings.whyItBreaks: git() now runs spawnSync without maxBuffer, so it uses Node's default of 1024*1024 bytes. git() produces the full patch via git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"]) at line 100; any diff over ~1 MiB (lockfiles, generated/minified assets, big refactors) exceeds the default. Verified on Node v24.15.0: when output exceeds maxBuffer, spawnSync returns status=null with error.code='ENOBUFS' and empty stderr. Because git() only checks `res.status !== 0` (null !== 0 is true) and reads only res.stderr, it throws `git diff <sha> HEAD failed: ` with no reason and the review aborts. The previous 64 MiB buffer handled these diffs; this is a regression on a core path of a diff-review tool.

findings.title: Removing git maxBuffer breaks review of diffs >1 MiB
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync's default maxBuffer is 1 MiB. When `git diff <base> HEAD` (line 100) produces more than 1 MiB, Node kills the child, truncates stdout, sets res.error=ERR_CHILD_PROCESS_STDIO_MAXBUFFER and res.status=null. The guard at line 12 (`res.status !== 0`) is true for null, so runLocal throws `git diff ... failed: ` with empty stderr (res.error is never read), and the entire local review of any large PR/lockfile/generated-file diff fails. Before this change the helper passed maxBuffer=64 MiB, so these diffs were reviewable; this is a regression on the primary path.

findings.title: Keep errored review check at failure, not neutral
findings.whyItBreaks: When review() throws, postCheck now concludes the "Needlefish" check run as "neutral" instead of "failure". neutral is a passing conclusion for required status checks, so a PR whose review errored can still satisfy branch protection and merge, even though the summary on line 193 still asserts "Review errored and did NOT pass this PR". The machine-readable gate (check conclusion) now contradicts the human-readable promise, silently converting an infrastructure failure into an approvable state.

findings.title: Don't downgrade review-failure check to neutral, unblocking merges
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch path for a failed/errored review now posts the 'Needlefish' check run with conclusion 'neutral' instead of 'failure'. GitHub branch protection treats a required status check with conclusion neutral (or skipped) as passing, so an infrastructure/review error that previously blocked merge now allows the PR to proceed — while the same payload still tells the user 'Review errored and did NOT pass this PR.' This is a silent failure-to-default downgrade on the tool's only machine-readable gate.

findings.title: Review-error check no longer blocks merge (failure downgraded to neutral)
findings.whyItBreaks: In the catch block the check-run conclusion was changed from "failure" to "neutral". GitHub treats a required status check with conclusion `neutral` (like `skipped`) as passing, whereas `failure` blocks the merge. The check-run name is the same "Needlefish" used for the real verdict, and VERDICT_CONCLUSION maps a blocking `changes_requested` to `failure` while only the non-blocking `needs_human` maps to `neutral` (lines 50-54), confirming `neutral` is the non-blocking state. The summary text still says "Review errored and did NOT pass this PR" (line 193), contradicting the new conclusion. Result: when review() or gh API calls throw (e.g. gh pr diff fails on an oversized/truncated PR, auth error, network), the merge gate silently opens instead of failing closed.

findings.title: Restore trusted-tool checkout; PR can now review itself
findings.whyItBreaks: The base workflow checked out the PR head into `target` and ran a trusted tool (`repository: frankekn/needlefish`, `ref: main`, path `needlefish`), explicitly to prevent a PR from controlling its own review (base review.yml:3-6, 44-70). The head revision deletes that second checkout and instead runs `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` from the PR-head checkout, so the reviewer binary/CLI logic executed against the PR is authored by the PR itself. A PR that rewrites src/cli.ts (or the review decision logic) to always report PASS silently neutralizes the review gate that guards its own merge. It also newly executes PR-authored code on a self-hosted runner: `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` now installs the PR head's dependencies (and any lifecycle scripts) and `src/cli.ts` runs with GH_TOKEN plus `pull-requests: write`/`checks: write` permissions, whereas previously only the trusted tool ran and the PR head was merely read as diff input. This is a real bypass even for same-repo PRs (the `if:` guard permits same-repo heads), and self-hosted runners persist state across jobs, raising the blast radius.
