findings.title: Restore severity normalization and conservative default in normalizeFinding
findings.whyItBreaks: Old code computed `sev = String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase()` and accepted any case/whitespace variant, defaulting unrecognized values to "P1". New code tests `raw.severity` directly, so `"p0"`, `" p1 "`, or `"P2\n"` (previously normalized to a valid severity) now fail the `SEVERITIES.includes` check and fall to the fallback, which was also changed from "P1" to "P3". Net effect: a raw review whose severity is a lowercase/padded P0/P1 — e.g. a genuine blocker — is silently reclassified as P3, and a finding with missing/absent severity also becomes P3 instead of P1. Since severity is what downstream verdict logic keys on (P0/P1 => blocking), this is a fail-open downgrade of a real severity signal.

findings.title: Restore severity normalization to avoid silent P3 downgrade
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version coerced the value with `String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase()` before the membership check, so model output such as `"p1"` or `" P2 "` was accepted and mapped to the correct severity. The new code tests `SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity as Severity)` against the raw, un-normalized value, so any lowercased or whitespace-padded severity fails the check and is silently returned as `"P3"` (lowest severity) instead. Concretely: raw.severity="p1" -> guard rejects -> returned severity "P3", so a P1 finding is reported as P3. The default change from "P1" to "P3" amplifies this by making every unrecognized value the least severe, which can suppress a serious finding from any downstream verdict logic.

findings.title: Restore severity normalization before SEVERITIES membership check
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding is exported and named as a normalizer, and normalizeReview feeds it untyped values (raw: any, findings.map(normalizeFinding)). The old body did String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase() before the SEVERITIES membership test; the new body tests raw.severity directly against exact-cased members. Any non-canonical severity (e.g. "p1", "p0", " P1 ", null/undefined/number) now fails the includes() check and is coerced to the default, which this diff also lowered from P1 to P3. So a critical finding emitted as "p0"/"p1" is silently downgraded to P3 (lowest severity) instead of being normalized to its intended severity, changing what downstream verdict/reporting logic sees.

findings.title: Restore credential scrubbing before spawning codex
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code built `env = { ...process.env }`, deleted GH_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN/GITHUB_API_TOKEN, and passed `env` to spawnSync. Head removes both the deletion and the `env` option, so spawnSync receives `env: undefined`. Per Node's child_process contract, an omitted `env` makes the child inherit the parent's full environment. The spawned `codex exec` agent (which runs tooling against the reviewed repo) therefore receives the parent's GitHub credentials, which it can read, echo into captured stdout/stderr, or exfiltrate over the network. This silently removes the only defense against credential leakage to the AI subprocess and its tool calls.

findings.title: Stop leaking GH/GITHUB tokens into spawned codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version built an env copy and explicitly deleted GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN and GITHUB_API_TOKEN before spawning, deliberately preventing the reviewed-code-executing codex child (and anything it spawns) from reading repo/CI credentials. This diff removes both the scrubbing and the `env` option, so spawnSync falls back to its default of inheriting the full process.env. Any credential in the parent environment (including the tokens that were intentionally withheld) is now exposed to the child process and its descendants.

findings.title: Restore GH token scrubbing before spawning codex
findings.whyItBreaks: The base built `env = { ...process.env }` and deleted GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN and GITHUB_API_TOKEN before spawnSync. This diff deletes those lines and drops the `env` option, so spawnSync now defaults to inheriting process.env verbatim. runCodex invokes an external AI agent (`codex exec`) that receives the prompt/repo content as input; any prompt-injection or tool behavior in that child can now read the CI credentials (which were previously guaranteed absent) and exfiltrate them. This is a deliberate secret-isolation control being removed on a changed line.

findings.title: Removing same-repo guard runs untrusted fork PR code on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The job keeps `runs-on: self-hosted` but the `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` guard was deleted, so the job now runs for pull_request events from forks. The workflow then checks out the fork's head (`ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}`) and executes PR-controlled code: `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (runs dependency lifecycle/postinstall scripts) and `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` (line 34), all on the persistent self-hosted runner. A fork author controls package.json/lockfile and src/, giving arbitrary code execution on the runner's host and any internal network it can reach.

findings.title: Restore fork guard: self-hosted runner now executes untrusted PR code
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the only control restricting this job to PRs whose head is the same repository. With it gone, the `pull_request` job runs for fork PRs too. The job runs on `runs-on: self-hosted` and (a) checks out the fork's `head.sha`, (b) runs `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` which executes the fork's dependency install/postinstall scripts, and (c) runs the fork's own `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` with `GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}`. Any external contributor can therefore run arbitrary code on the self-hosted runner, a persistent machine that typically has broader host/network/credential access than a GitHub-hosted runner. GitHub explicitly warns against self-hosted runners for untrusted (fork) PRs.

findings.title: Restore fork-PR guard before self-hosted runner executes PR code
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the only control keeping fork PRs off the self-hosted runner. With it gone, the `pull_request` job runs for any fork, checking out attacker-controlled head code (`ref: ...head.sha`) and executing it: `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` runs the PR's dependency lifecycle/postinstall scripts, then `tsx src/cli.ts` runs the PR's own `src/`. That is arbitrary code execution on self-hosted infrastructure by anyone who can open a PR, plus `GH_TOKEN: secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN` is exported into the untrusted step's environment. A self-hosted runner typically has persistent credentials and network reach, so this is a security bypass, not just CI noise.

findings.title: readRunnerDurationMs now silently replaces a valid 0 duration with the fallback
findings.whyItBreaks: 0 is a finite, non-negative duration and was explicitly accepted before this PR (`parsed >= 0`). With `parsed > 0`, `readRunnerDurationMs("0", 5000)` now returns 5000 and `readRunnerDurationMs("0", 2000)` returns 2000. On the live path these constants are consumed by `setTimeout(..., RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS)` (@src/shared/runner-process.ts:124) and `setTimeout(..., RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS)` (@src/shared/runner-process.ts:123). So an operator who sets `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0` (escalate SIGTERM→SIGKILL immediately) or `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0` (stop waiting for child close immediately) now gets the default 5000ms/2000ms instead — the explicit configuration is silently ignored and process teardown is delayed by up to 7s. No doc, test, or code comment in the repo declares 0 invalid, so the change is an unexplained behavior regression rather than a fix for a hang (grace=0 still schedules SIGKILL and the 2s give-up still fires).

findings.title: readRunnerDurationMs now silently ignores an explicit 0 duration
findings.whyItBreaks: Base accepted any finite non-negative value (`parsed >= 0`), so setting NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 or NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 was honored: grace 0 escalates to SIGKILL immediately after SIGTERM, and give-up 0 resolves right after SIGKILL. With `parsed > 0`, `Number('0')` is 0, the predicate is false, and the function returns fallbackMs instead — so RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS @src/shared/runner-process.ts:124 silently becomes 5000ms and RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS @src/shared/runner-process.ts:123 silently becomes 2000ms. The operator's explicit 0 is discarded with no warning, a behavior regression versus base for a previously-valid value.

findings.title: Restore coverage backstop so unmapped changed files are still reviewed
findings.whyItBreaks: reviewLarge now goes straight from `sortByRisk(mapResult.hotspots).slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS)` (MAX_HOTSPOTS=6 @src/core/review.ts:26) into the deep loop. The deleted backstop collected every changedFile not present in a selected hotspot into a tail hotspot and deep-reviewed it. Now any changed file the map pass did not assign to a surface — or any file in a hotspot ranked below the top 6 — is never deep-reviewed, and because residual_risks is hardcoded to [] no residual risk records the gap. The review still returns a normal-looking verdict, so a reviewer believes all changed files were covered when they were silently skipped. This directly violates the removed comment's stated invariant ("never silently skip a changed file").

findings.title: Propagate deep-pass residual risks instead of hardcoding an empty list
findings.whyItBreaks: candidateMerged.residual_risks is now hardcoded to [] and the prior `residuals.push(...res.residual_risks)` (base review.ts, deep-loop body) was deleted. Each deep pass can return residual risks carrying `blocks:true`; those previously flowed into candidateMerged and on to `deriveVerdict(pruned.findings, pruned.residual_risks)` @src/core/review.ts:122. Now the critic is handed an empty residual list, so unless the critic independently re-derives them, blocking signals from deep passes are lost and the final verdict can report pass/merge despite a deep pass having flagged a blocking gap.

findings.title: Keep deep-pass failure isolation in the large-review loop
findings.whyItBreaks: The per-hotspot try/catch was removed, so `normalizeReview(extractJson(runCodex(...)))` @src/core/review.ts:103 now runs unguarded. runCodex is an external model call per hotspot (up to MAX_HOTSPOTS=6); previously one failing hotspot was caught, logged into checked, and recorded as a blocking residual while the remaining hotspots still produced findings. Now any single transient failure throws out of reviewLarge, discarding every finding and checked entry already collected and failing the whole review — a large PR's review degrades from partial-with-blocking-note to total failure.

findings.title: Restore tail-coverage backstop so no changed file is skipped
findings.whyItBreaks: This PR deletes the coverage backstop that appended a 'tail-coverage' hotspot for any changed file not assigned to a selected hotspot (base version 211dff8:src/core/review.ts:98-110). reviewLarge is a live path (review() routes here when patch > 30000 chars or changedFiles > 10, lines 29-31/132), and hotspots are capped at MAX_HOTSPOTS=6 (line 93). After this change, changed files the map pass never assigned to a surface, and any files inside hotspots 7+, receive no deep review at all and produce no finding or residual risk. The review then returns a verdict built only from the reviewed hotspots, so it can emit PASS/clean while entire changed files were never inspected — the exact 'silently skip a changed file' failure the deleted comment guarded against.

findings.title: Deep-pass residual risks are dropped before reaching the critic/result
findings.whyItBreaks: residual_risks is now hardcoded to [] and the per-hotspot `residuals.push(...res.residual_risks)` collection was removed (base 211dff8:src/core/review.ts:115,127). candidateMerged is serialized into the critic prompt via {{FINDINGS}} (line 116), and in the large path the critic only receives patchStat, not the diff, so it cannot independently rediscover these. Every residual risk a deep pass reported — including the blocking 'file(s) not deep-reviewed' signal that used to be recorded on a failed pass — is now discarded: it reaches neither the critic nor the final residualRisks (which is taken only from pruned.residual_risks at line 128). A caller therefore sees an empty/partial residual-risk set indistinguishable from 'no residual risks', potentially reporting PASS on a review with unexamined risk.

findings.title: Restore tail-coverage backstop for changed files not in a hotspot
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff deletes the tail-coverage backstop that appended an extra hotspot for changed files not present in the selected hotspots. hotspots is truncated to MAX_HOTSPOTS at line 93, so any changed file belonging to a truncated-away (or unmapped) hotspot is no longer deep-reviewed at all; the file is silently skipped instead of reviewed. The removed comment explicitly promised 'never silently skip a changed file'. Consumers of deep review now receive a hotspot set that may omit changed files, so real defects in those files never reach the critic/verdict.

findings.title: Propagate deep-pass residual_risks instead of hardcoding []
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff removes the residuals accumulator and the `residuals.push(...res.residual_risks)` collection, and hardcodes candidateMerged.residual_risks to []. Deep-review residual risks (including blocks:true entries that should force a BLOCK verdict) are therefore dropped before the critic prompt is built at line 115-117. The critic only sees the candidate passed via {{FINDINGS}}, so it cannot carry those blocking risks forward, and the final verdict derived at line 122 from pruned.residual_risks can be PASS where the deep passes had flagged a blocking risk. Failure/blocking signal is silently discarded.

findings.title: Restore focus injection in large-PR deep and map prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff deletes .replace("{{FOCUS}}", bundle.focus ?? "(none)") from the deep prompt and deletes focus/deep from mapBundle. deep.md still carries the template line 'Focus: {{FOCUS}} (if not "(none)", prioritize findings in that area)' (prompts/deep.md:96), so the deep pass now sends the literal token {{FOCUS}} and no focus guidance; map.md:37 ('If a `focus` field is set (not null), rank matching surfaces higher') can no longer see focus because mapBundle omits it. Net effect: the user-facing --focus option is silently ignored on exactly the large-PR path where lens-narrowing matters, and a raw template artifact leaks into the model prompt.

findings.title: Restore {{FOCUS}} substitution or drop the placeholder from deep.md
findings.whyItBreaks: At base, reviewLarge built the deep prompt with `.replace("{{FOCUS}}", bundle.focus ?? "(none)")`, so prompts/deep.md defines a {{FOCUS}} slot that receives the user's focus guidance. This PR deletes that replacement, and prompts/deep.md is not in the patch (patchStat lists only src/core/review.ts), so the template still contains {{FOCUS}} and the string sent to runCodex now includes the literal token "{{FOCUS}}" instead of the focus text. Net effect: for large PRs the focus input is silently ignored (and a stray placeholder is injected into the model prompt), while reviewSmall (line 54, JSON.stringify(bundle)) still forwards focus, so the same input works for small PRs and is dropped for large ones. The same removal at lines 83-89 also drops focus/deep from mapBundle, so the map pass no longer sees them either.

findings.title: Restore focus/deep forwarding in the large-review path
findings.whyItBreaks: This PR deletes the only reads of bundle.focus/bundle.deep in reviewLarge: `focus`/`deep` were removed from `mapBundle` (old lines 89-90, now ending at agentsMd on line 88) and `.replace("{{FOCUS}}", bundle.focus ?? "(none)")` was removed from the deep prompt chain. reviewSmall still stringifies the whole bundle (including focus) into review.md at src/core/review.ts:52-56, so the same `focus` input is honored for small PRs but silently dropped for large PRs (patch > 30000 chars or > 10 files, src/core/review.ts:30-31) — exactly the case where focus matters most. With the substitution gone, the deep.md template is also handed a literal `{{FOCUS}}` token instead of the user's focus text (or `(none)`), so the deep pass receives no focus guidance and no signal that focus was requested.

findings.title: Fix duration rounding producing '1m 60s' / '60s'
findings.whyItBreaks: minutes is now floored from raw ms (`Math.floor(ms / 60000)`) while seconds independently rounds the remainder (`Math.round((ms % 60000) / 1000)`), so the remainder can round up to 60 instead of carrying into minutes. For ms = 119500 (any ms in [119500, 119999]) this yields '1m 60s'; for ms in [59500, 59999] it yields '60s' where the base implementation emitted '1m 0s'. These strings are rendered into the stats line at src/shared/render.ts:75 and :80, so the PR's own duration values can be displayed incorrectly/malformed.

findings.title: formatDuration can emit "60s" / "Xm 60s" after independent rounding
findings.whyItBreaks: Minutes are floored from raw ms while seconds are rounded from the remainder, so the rounded seconds can reach 60. For ms=59999: minutes=Math.floor(59999/60000)=0, seconds=Math.round(59999%60000/1000)=Math.round(59.999)=60 -> "60s" (old code produced "1m 0s"). For ms=119999: minutes=1, seconds=Math.round(59999/1000)=60 -> "1m 60s" (old code produced "2m 0s"). Any ms in [59500,59999] + k*60000 hits this. These values are rendered to users via renderMarkdown's stats line (src/shared/render.ts:75 and :80), so the report shows a non-normalized, previously-impossible duration string.

findings.title: formatDuration can emit invalid "Xm 60s" after rounding
findings.whyItBreaks: minutes is floored from the full ms and seconds is rounded independently, so when ms % 60000 >= 59500 seconds rounds up to 60 instead of carrying into minutes. formatDuration(119999) returns "1m 60s" and formatDuration(3599999) returns "59m 60s"; the base implementation normalized these to "2m 0s" and "60m 0s". The result is rendered directly into the stats line of the markdown report (src/shared/render.ts:75 and :80), so users see a nonsensical duration.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger now accepts 0, contradicting its positive contract
findings.whyItBreaks: The guard changed from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0`, so the input "0" no longer throws and is returned as a valid value. The function is exported (public API), its name promises a positive integer, and the thrown message still says `requires a positive integer`, yet 0 is not positive. Callers that rely on the documented positivity guarantee (e.g. to size a count/timeout/retry budget) silently receive 0 instead of an error, conflating an invalid input with a legitimate value. No in-repo caller exists, but for an exported carrier the promise itself is the contract.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger now accepts 0, contradicting its positive-integer contract
findings.whyItBreaks: The guard was changed to reject only `parsed < 0`, so `0` is now returned as valid. `Number("")`, `Number(" ")` and `Number("\n")` all coerce to 0, so an empty/blank flag value (e.g. a timeout, attempt count, or size parsed via this helper) silently passes validation and yields 0 instead of the previous `requires a positive integer` error. The exported symbol name and the throw message on line 33 both promise a positive integer, so the implementation and its public contract now disagree; callers trust the promise and receive an unusable zero.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger now accepts 0, contradicting its documented contract
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported validator promises a positive integer: the symbol name is `parsePositiveInteger` (src/shared/runner.ts:30) and the error text says `requires a positive integer` (src/shared/runner.ts:33). Changing `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0` makes the body accept 0, so the promise (validation of positivity) is not implemented by the body. Concretely, `Number('')`, `Number(' ')`, and `Number('0')` all become 0 and are now returned silently instead of throwing, so a caller parsing a count/timeout/attempt value (e.g. from an env var that is unset/empty) receives 0 where it previously got a fail-fast error, and every downstream consumer that relies on the documented positivity guarantee (count, divisor, timeout, retry attempts) now operates on 0.
